description: We are a team of programmers from Stevens Institute of Technology, based in New Jersey.
summary: Offworld Atlas is an interactive web atlas that searches the whole Earth for places that could stand in for future Moon base sites and Mars landing sites. It shows 84 places: 62 new candidates in 29 countries, for which our literature search found no published analog study, and 22 already-studied analogs kept for reference. Each place is measured with open NASA and ESA data (terrain, land cover, climate, ground temperature and surface minerals) and compared, one trait at a time, with seven real Moon and Mars sites, including Mons Malapert and Jezero Crater. The challenge asks for new analogs that are well characterized, so every place explains why it might be an analog, where the likeness breaks down, and what a mission team could test there. Visitors can rank every place against a base, fly a drone over real terrain, take a guided tour and find candidates in their own country. We also tested our scoring against control places such as rainforest and farmland, and the app states where the method fails. It matters because it points mission teams to untested places beyond the widely studied analog sites.
details:
What it is

Offworld Atlas is an interactive web atlas that searches the whole Earth for places that could stand in for future Moon base sites and Mars landing sites. It shows 84 places. 62 are new candidates in 29 countries, for which our literature search found no published analog study. The other 22 are already-studied analogs, kept for reference. Every place is measured with open NASA and ESA data and compared, one trait at a time, with seven real Moon and Mars sites.

How it works

  1. Screen. We screened global data on climate, remoteness and young volcanoes, and added landforms that matter for exploration (impact craters, lava tubes, wind-carved ridges, salt pans and frozen ground). We kept the places with no published analog study.
  2. Measure. A Python pipeline measures the 51 km around each place: terrain from the Copernicus DEM, land cover from ESA WorldCover, surface water from the JRC, climate from NASA POWER, ground temperature from NASA MODIS and surface minerals from NASA EMIT.
  3. Compare. The same terrain measures are computed for seven Moon and Mars sites from NASA's LOLA and MOLA elevation models, with ground temperatures from the LRO Diviner instrument and from the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers.
  4. Check. We test the scoring against control places chosen to be unlike the Moon and Mars, and the app states where the method fails.

Features

1. The atlas: 84 places on a globe in space

The atlas opens on a globe with a numbered bubble for each continent. As you zoom in, each bubble splits into regions and then into named places. New candidates are marked in yellow, studied analogs are shown dimmer, and one switch hides everything except the new candidates.

2. A guided tour that tells the story

Eight stops explain what an analog is, visit a famous one, show how we screened the Earth, fly to the best new Mars candidate, and end with what Earth cannot reproduce. The tour moves the map itself, and every number in its captions is read live from the app's data.

3. Every place explains itself

Selecting a place flies down to a 3D view of its real terrain. The panel says why the place might be an analog, lists the evidence with a link to each source, and states plainly whether the place is already studied or is a new candidate that has not been tested in the field.

4. Similarity scores, one trait at a time

Each place is compared with a chosen Moon or Mars site on 11 measured traits, including slope, flat ground for landing, relief, roughness at several scales, bare ground, dryness and ground temperature. The panel shows where the two are similar, partly similar and different. For example, Laguna Salada in Mexico scores 74% overall against Jezero Crater: its relief is almost identical (1,767 m against 1,775 m), while the air overhead scores 0%. The percentages say how alike two places are. They are not the chance that a place is a good analog.

5. Rock and mineral chemistry

The app compares the mapped rock family of each place with the Moon or Mars site, and compares the mineral groups detected by NASA's EMIT instrument on the International Space Station with the groups reported at Jezero and Gale craters. Where the maps cannot support a conclusion, the app says so.

6. What you could test here

Each place lists up to three things a mission team could rehearse there, such as salt detection, driving on lava, cave entry or cold-weather operations, with the measured reason and the travel time to the nearest city. These are worked out by rule from the landform and the measurements. They are starting points, not published test plans.

7. Places like this one

An Earth-to-Earth search compares each place with the other 83 on measured terrain, bare ground, rain, ground temperature and rock family, and lists the five closest. It links new candidates to studied analogs: Laguna Salada's closest matches include Yungay in the Atacama Desert, one of the best-known Mars analogs.

8. A ranking, and a check on our own method

Every place can be ranked against any of the seven Moon and Mars sites. To test the scoring, we also used data from eight control places chosen to be unlike the Moon and Mars: rainforest, farmland, forest and wetland. Against Mons Malapert, known Moon analogs average 27% and the controls 11%. Against Jezero Crater the figures are 57% and 35%. Against Arcadia Planitia the method fails, with 45% and 47%, and the app says so.

9. Data layers on the site and on the globe

In a site view, slope, roughness, land cover and surface water can be draped over the terrain for the measured 51 km square.

On the globe, imagery from NASA Worldview shows land surface temperature by day and night, snow cover, dust, vegetation and a recent satellite view, next to layers for climate, travel time to cities and young volcanoes.

10. Drone view over real terrain

Any place can be flown over in a free-flight drone view built from real elevation data and satellite imagery. A live readout gives the slope, roughness, land cover and water under the drone, and the same data layers can be switched on in flight.

11. Real sunlight, night and the Moon

The positions of the Sun and the Moon and the night side of the Earth are calculated for any date and time. Site views and the drone view are lit from the real direction of the Sun, and a time-lapse runs at 1, 6 or 12 hours per second.

12. Candidates near you

A country picker lists the places in any of the 31 countries in the atlas, starting with the visitor's own country where we have one, and a second button finds the five places nearest to the visitor. The location is only used in the browser to measure distances.

Benefits and intended impact

  • For mission teams and researchers: a shortlist of untested places beyond the handful of famous analog sites, each with its data, what could be tested there and how long it takes to reach.
  • For students and the public: people in 29 countries can find a candidate analog in their own country and see why it resembles another world.
  • For anyone repeating the work: the pipeline is open, so any coordinates on Earth can be measured and scored the same way.

What makes it creative

  • It looks for new places, where most analog lists repeat the well-known ones.
  • It tests its own scoring against control places and publishes the case where the scoring fails.
  • It gives a score for each trait, because an analog does not have to match everything. Mount Suswa in Kenya is green and wet, nothing like the Moon, but its lava tube caves are the reason it is in the atlas.
  • It turns the data into something you can explore: a drone flight, real sunlight, and a story told by the map.

What we considered

  • Honest wording. "New candidate" means our search found no published analog study. It does not mean nobody has ever looked, and none of the candidates has been tested in the field.
  • Earth's limits. No place on Earth has the Moon's vacuum, one-sixth gravity or radiation, or the thin air of Mars. The app shows gravity and air pressure side by side and leaves planet-wide properties out of the overall score.
  • What is not compared yet. Ice, dust, biology and caves are measured for the Earth places but are not yet scored against the Moon or Mars.
  • Measurement against model. Most figures are measurements. The ground temperature for Arcadia Planitia comes from a climate model, and the app labels it as calculated.
  • Accuracy. The descriptions of 72 places were checked against their cited sources, and 23 were corrected.
  • Licenses. Every dataset is credited in the app, and no restricted imagery is stored in the project.

Tools, languages and software

  • Web app: TypeScript, React and Vite, with MapLibre GL JS for the globe and maps, three.js for the drone view, and plain CSS.
  • Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Shapely, h5py and Pillow.
  • Artwork: Blender, rendering real elevation data of Mount Suswa.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages, built and published by GitHub Actions.
